stem: A newborn with prenatal opioid exposure is being monitored for neonatal withdrawal. Which finding is most consistent with neonatal abstinence syndrome/neonatal opioid withdrawal?

options.A: Tremors, irritability or high-pitched crying, and poor feeding
options.B: Persistent flaccidity with no irritability or feeding difficulty
options.C: Isolated jaundice as the only expected withdrawal manifestation
options.D: No possible symptoms because prenatal opioid exposure cannot cause neonatal withdrawal

rationale: CDC states that neonatal abstinence syndrome can occur when newborns withdraw from substances including opioids after prenatal exposure. Signs can include tremors, irritability or excessive/high-pitched crying, and poor feeding or sucking. Therefore A is correct. Not every exposed newborn has the same signs or severity, and the other options do not represent the characteristic withdrawal pattern.
educational_objective: Recognize common neonatal opioid-withdrawal findings after prenatal opioid exposure.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_locator: Neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS): opioid use during pregnancy can lead to NAS in some newborns; withdrawal signs may include tremors, irritability/high-pitched crying, and poor feeding/sucking
source_claim_supported: Prenatal opioid exposure can lead to neonatal withdrawal, with signs including tremors, high-pitched crying/irritability and poor feeding.

correction_summary: Reframed the item to avoid implying that every opioid-exposed newborn develops NAS or that withdrawal has a single-system presentation. Anchored the signs directly to current CDC guidance and removed unnecessary treatment claims.
audit_findings: A directly matches CDC-listed signs. B, C and D conflict with the recognized withdrawal pattern. The stem states monitoring after prenatal exposure rather than assuming diagnosis solely from exposure. No second-answer ambiguity, cueing or unsupported precision remains.
